newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Telecoms to China plump ex-Nordic air cargo flows.
newsitem.headline: Telecoms to China plump ex-Nordic air cargo flows.

text.p: The success of Swedish telecommunications firm LM Ericsson AB in China fuelled the fastest growing segment of air cargo exports from the Nordic region, an analyst said on Friday.

In the latest comprehensive report commissioned by regional aviation authorities in Sweden, Denmark, Norway and Finland with 1995 data, Swedish exports made up almost half of outbound air cargo traffic from the Nordic region at 117,900 tonnes.

Exports to China from Sweden by air totalled 6,400 tonnes, an increase of over 100 percent, and this was seen continuing, said Lars-Gunnar Comen, author of the report entitled "The Nordic Air Cargo Market".
Swedish exports to the Far East accounted for 28.2 percent, an increase of 45.5 percent from 1994, the report said.
"The main reason for the boom to China is Ericsson Radio and Ericsson Telecom," Comen said.
"As far as I understand Ericsson will continue its very good marketing efforts in China...heavy demand for air cargo space to China will continue and could even increase."

Export air cargo volumes in 1995 from the Nordic region totalled 253,500 tonnes, said the report, compiled on behalf of Swedish and Finnish civil aviation authorities, New Oslo Airport Gardermoen and Copenhagen Airports.
Of the total, Sweden accounted for 47 percent, Denmark 22 percent, Norway 17 percent and Finland the remaining 14 percent.

The biggest destination for cargo from this part of the world was the Far East, with 35.6 percent of the total ending up there. Next largest were air cargo exports to North America, at 22.6 percent, followed by Europe at 19.9 percent.
Exports to Latin America by air accounted for 7.3 percent of the total. No comparison figures for 1994 were available.
Air exports from Denmark to the Far East totalled 27.5 percent and to Europe, 20.2 percent.
"In Sweden the market is dominated by five to 10 big multi-national companies. In Denmark there's not a dominating company," Comen said.
He pointed out that the picture was the same if you looked at the number of freight forwarders in Denmark compared to in Sweden, where the market was made up of far fewer players.
"It seems to be their way of doing business -- they don't have as many large companies but many small ones," Comen said.
From Norway, 58.8 percent of air cargo exports were to the Far East, with 17,610 tonnes of the Far Eastern total of 27,450 tonnes going to Japan.
"The Norwegian market is very heavily dependent on the salmon traffic. There is a lot of fish going -- especially to Japan -- but also to some other Asia countries," Comen said.

From Finland, European air exports were highest at 31.1 percent followed by the Far East at 29.3 percent. Finnish telecoms group Nokia Oy and other high-tech companies were the largest buyers of air cargo space, Comen said.
Its proximity to Russia made Europe a key destination for Finnish air cargo volumes, Comen said.
"There is a large proportion going to Russia and the CIS countries. Since that is included in Europe, that might be one part of the explanation," he said.
